title: Generative AI for Coding
description: Using an AI assistant to write, read, debug and document code, including if you do not yet code.

lessons.title: AI coding assistants
lessons.description: The three shapes, what they are good at, and the three rules that keep it safe.
lessons.content:
## Learn

This module is for everyone, including people who do not write code. Reading and understanding code is a large part of what these tools help with, and that is useful to anyone who occasionally has to look at a script someone sent them.

### The three shapes

**In your editor.** Suggestions as you type, chat about the file you have open, changes proposed across several files. GitHub Copilot and similar.

**In a chat tool.** Paste code, ask questions, get code back. Works with any general assistant and needs nothing installed. This is where to start.

**Agentic assistants.** Given a task, they read your project, make changes across files, run commands and iterate. Powerful, and they require more judgement about what to let them do.

For this module, a chat tool is enough. Everything here works by pasting code into any assistant.

### What they are genuinely good at

**Explaining code.** The most valuable and least appreciated use, and the one most relevant to non-programmers.

**Boilerplate.** Repetitive, well-understood code that takes time and no thought.

**Translating between languages.** You know what you want in one language and need it in another.

**Tests.** Patterned, tedious, and something they do well.

**Debugging.** Give it the code, the error and what you expected.

**Documentation.** Turning working code into readable explanation.

### What they are bad at

**Knowing your intent.** They see your code, not what you meant. A confident completion of the wrong thing is easy to accept.

**Anything genuinely novel.** They produce variations on patterns they have seen. Hard, original problems are not their strength.

**Your codebase's conventions**, unless you show them.

**Being right about libraries they know less well.** Invented functions are common, especially in smaller libraries.

### The discipline

Three rules, and they are the whole of safe AI-assisted coding.

**1. Read everything before you accept it.** Everything it writes becomes your responsibility. Accepting unread is a habit that forms within a week and costs later.

**2. Run it.** Generated code that looks right and does not work is the normal case, not the exception. Module 2's debugging exercises were not decoration.

**3. Understand it, or do not ship it.** If you cannot explain what a line does, you cannot maintain it, debug it, or judge whether it is safe. Ask until you can.

### On sensitive code

Understand what your tool sends and what your organisation permits before using it on proprietary code. This is a real policy question in most workplaces, and worth asking before rather than after.

## Demonstrate

Take any code you did not write. If you have none, use this:

```python
def process(items):
    result = []
    for i in range(len(items)):
        if items[i] not in result:
            result.append(items[i])
    return result
```

Ask four questions in sequence:

1. *"Explain what this does, to someone who does not know Python."*
2. *"What could go wrong with this?"*
3. *"Is there a simpler way to write it?"*
4. *"What would break if the input were very large?"*

Question 2 is the most useful and least used. Question 4 surfaces the real problem here: this is much slower than it needs to be on large inputs, because `in result` scans the whole list every time.

You now know something about the code that reading it would not have told you quickly.

## Practice

Find a piece of code in your own life -- a script from a colleague, something from a tutorial, a formula-heavy spreadsheet macro, anything.

Run the four questions.

Then do the essential part: **verify one specific claim** from the explanation against the actual documentation. Pick something it asserted about what a function does.

Record whether it was right. This habit -- verify one claim per explanation -- is what keeps this safe.

## What to remember

- Useful even if you do not write code; explaining is the underrated use
- Good at boilerplate, translation, tests, debugging and documentation
- Bad at your intent, genuinely novel problems, and less common libraries
- Read it, run it, understand it -- or do not ship it
- Check what your organisation permits before using it on work code

lessons.title: Generating code
lessons.description: Brief it properly: language, input, output, edge cases, constraints, style.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Getting good code out of a model is mostly about the brief, exactly as in module 4.

### What a good request contains

**The language and version.** Python 3.12 behaves differently from Python 3.8.

**The input, precisely.** Types, shapes, what the data actually looks like. Give a real example.

**The output, precisely.** What comes back, in what form.

**The edge cases.** Empty input, missing values, duplicates, wrong types. If you do not say, you get code that breaks on the first one.

**The constraints.** No external libraries, must work on large inputs, must not modify the original, must handle errors rather than raise.

**The style.** Type hints, docstrings, how errors should be reported.

A weak request:

> Write a function to clean up a list of emails.

A strong one:

> Python 3.11. Write a function that takes a list of strings which may contain email addresses, and returns a list of unique, valid, lowercased addresses in the order first seen.
>
> - Strip surrounding whitespace
> - Treat addresses differing only by case as the same
> - Skip anything without exactly one `@` with text either side
> - Return an empty list for an empty input, do not raise
> - No external libraries
> - Type hints and a docstring

The second produces usable code in one attempt. The first produces something you will spend ten minutes correcting.

### Ask for the awkward cases explicitly

The most common cause of broken generated code is an unstated edge case. Adding one line -- *"handle empty input, duplicates and malformed entries; say in a comment what you assumed"* -- catches most of it.

The "say what you assumed" part is valuable. It surfaces decisions the model made silently that you might disagree with.

### Ask for tests at the same time

> Also write tests covering: the normal case, empty input, duplicates, and one malformed entry.

Tests do two things. They check the code, and they tell you what the model *thought* the code should do -- which sometimes differs from what you meant, visibly.

### Small pieces, not whole programs

Asking for an entire application produces something plausible and hard to verify. Asking for one function with a clear contract produces something you can read, test and trust.

Build up from pieces you understand. This is slower to start and much faster overall.

## Demonstrate

Write the same request twice and compare.

**Weak.** *"Write a function to parse dates from text."*

**Strong.**

> Python 3.11. Write a function that extracts dates from a string and returns them as `datetime.date` objects, in the order they appear.
>
> - Accept `DD/MM/YYYY` and `YYYY-MM-DD` only
> - Ignore anything that looks like a date but is invalid, such as `32/01/2024`
> - Return an empty list if none are found
> - Standard library only
> - Type hints and a docstring
> - Note in a comment any assumption you had to make
>
> Also write tests for: both formats, an invalid date, no dates at all, and two dates in one string.

Run both. The weak version will make silent choices about formats and ambiguity, and you will not know which. The strong version will state its assumption about `01/02/2024` -- which is the real problem with date parsing and the thing you needed to be told.

## Practice

### Exercise: brief it properly

Pick a small function you actually need, or use this: a function that takes a list of dictionaries representing orders and returns the total value per customer, as a dictionary.

Write the weak version of the request. Then write the strong version with all six ingredients.

Run both. Compare the code, and specifically compare how each handles a missing `amount` key.

```python
def totals_by_customer(orders: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Total order value per customer.

    Each order is a dict with 'customer' (str) and 'amount' (number).
    Orders missing either key are skipped. Returns an empty dict for
    an empty input.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for `[{"customer": "a", "amount": 10}, {"customer": "a", "amount": 5}, {"customer": "b", "amount": 3}]`:

```
{'a': 15.0, 'b': 3.0}
```

:::hint Getting started
A dict accumulator and one loop. For each order, check both keys are present before using them -- `if "customer" not in order or "amount" not in order: continue`. Use `totals.get(name, 0.0) + amount` to accumulate, or `collections.defaultdict(float)` if you prefer.
:::

:::solution
```python
def totals_by_customer(orders: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Total order value per customer."""
    totals: dict[str, float] = {}

    for order in orders:
        customer = order.get("customer")
        amount = order.get("amount")
        # Skip malformed rows rather than raising: one bad row in a large
        # import should not lose the whole batch.
        if not isinstance(customer, str) or not isinstance(amount, (int, float)):
            continue
        totals[customer] = totals.get(customer, 0.0) + float(amount)

    return totals


if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = [
        {"customer": "a", "amount": 10},
        {"customer": "a", "amount": 5},
        {"customer": "b", "amount": 3},
        {"customer": "c"},
    ]
    print(totals_by_customer(data))
```

Output:

```
{'a': 15.0, 'b': 3.0}
```

The `isinstance` checks rather than a bare key check catch a second class of bad data: an amount that arrived as a string. Note also that `isinstance(True, int)` is `True` in Python, so a boolean amount would slip through -- worth knowing, and worth a comment if your data could contain one.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This is a plausible piece of generated code for counting word frequencies. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def word_counts(text: str) -> dict[str, int]:
    counts = {}
    for word in text.split():
        word = word.lower().strip(".,!?")
        counts[word] = counts[word] + 1
    return counts
```

:::hint What to look at
Run it mentally on `"Hello world"`. Then run it on `"Hello, hello!"` and think about what `strip` does versus what you might expect.
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: `counts[word]` on a word not yet seen raises `KeyError`.** It fails on the very first word. Use `counts.get(word, 0) + 1`.

**Bug two: stripping punctuation can produce an empty string.** A token that is only punctuation -- a stray `--` or `...` -- strips to `""`, which is then counted as a word. Skip empties.

```python
def word_counts(text: str) -> dict[str, int]:
    """Count word frequencies, lowercased and stripped of edge punctuation."""
    counts: dict[str, int] = {}

    for token in text.split():
        word = token.lower().strip(".,!?;:\"'")
        if not word:
            continue
        counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1

    return counts
```

Bug one fails loudly on the first call, so you would catch it immediately. Bug two is the instructive one: it never raises, and it quietly adds a phantom empty-string entry to your results. Loud bugs are cheap. Quiet ones are what you write tests for.
:::

## What to remember

- Language and version, exact input and output, edge cases, constraints, style
- Always state the awkward cases or you get code that breaks on the first one
- Ask it to state its assumptions; that is where silent decisions surface
- Ask for tests at the same time -- they reveal what it thought you meant
- Small functions with clear contracts, not whole programs

lessons.title: Explaining code
lessons.description: The best thing these tools do, and the one useful to non-programmers.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Explaining code is the best thing these tools do, and the most useful capability in this module for someone who is not a programmer.

### Why it works so well

Explanation is **transformation**, not recall. The code is right there. The model is turning one representation into another, which is exactly the safe category from module 3.

It still gets things wrong -- particularly claims about what a specific library function does, which is recall wearing a disguise. But the structural explanation is usually reliable.

### The questions worth asking

**"Explain this line by line to someone who does not know this language."** The baseline. Specifying the audience matters as much here as anywhere.

**"What is the purpose of this, in one sentence?"** Forces a summary rather than a walkthrough, which is often what you actually wanted.

**"What could go wrong with this?"** The best question in this module. Surfaces edge cases, failure modes and assumptions.

**"What would break if the input were very large / empty / malformed?"** Specific versions of the above.

**"Why might someone have written it this way rather than the obvious way?"** Often reveals a real constraint you could not see.

**"What does this depend on that is not in this file?"** Useful for understanding a fragment out of context.

**"Rewrite this with comments explaining each step, but do not change the behaviour."** Gives you an annotated version to keep.

### Working with unfamiliar code

A sequence that works well for code you have inherited:

1. **Purpose first.** One sentence, whole thing.
2. **Structure.** "What are the main parts and how do they relate?"
3. **The confusing part.** Paste the specific bit and ask about it.
4. **The vocabulary.** "What does this term mean in this context?"
5. **The risks.** "What would I need to be careful about if I changed this?"

Top-down, then into detail. Much better than line-by-line from the start, which buries the shape in detail.

### Verification

The explanation will be structurally right and may be factually wrong about specifics.

The habit: **verify one claim per explanation.** Pick something specific it asserted about a function or a behaviour and check the documentation.

You will find it is usually right. The occasional time it is not is the one that matters, and the habit is what catches it.

### For learning a language

This is a genuinely good way to learn. Take code in a language you are learning, ask for an explanation, then ask "how would I write this in [language you know]?" The comparison teaches faster than either alone.

## Demonstrate

Take this, which is deliberately unclear:

```python
def f(d, k, v=None):
    return {**d, k: v} if v is not None else {i: j for i, j in d.items() if i != k}
```

Ask, in order:

1. *"What does this do, in one sentence?"*
2. *"Explain it line by line to someone who knows basic Python but not this syntax."*
3. *"What is `{**d, k: v}` doing?"*
4. *"What could go wrong with this?"*
5. *"Rewrite it clearly, without changing the behaviour."*

Question 5 usually produces something far more readable, which is a good argument for asking it about any code you have to maintain.

Question 4 should surface that the function does two unrelated things depending on whether `v` is `None`, which is a design problem rather than a bug -- and exactly the kind of thing a reviewer would say.

## Practice

Take the most confusing piece of code you can find in your own world.

Run the five-step sequence for unfamiliar code: purpose, structure, the confusing part, the vocabulary, the risks.

Then verify one specific claim against documentation.

Write two sentences: what the code does, and what you would be careful about changing. If you can write those two sentences, the exercise worked.

## What to remember

- Explanation is transformation, which is the safe category
- "What could go wrong with this?" is the best question available
- Go top-down: purpose, structure, detail -- not line by line from the start
- Specify the audience for the explanation, as with any prompt
- Verify one specific claim per explanation against real documentation

lessons.title: Debugging with AI
lessons.description: Four things to include, and why quiet bugs are the expensive kind.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Debugging is one of the strongest uses, provided you give it what it needs.

### What to include

Four things. Missing any one makes the answer a guess.

**1. The code.** Enough context, not just the failing line.

**2. The actual error, in full.** The complete traceback, not "it says there is an error". The traceback is the most informative thing you have.

**3. What you expected.** The model cannot know your intent.

**4. What actually happened.** The real output or behaviour.

Plus, when relevant: what you have already tried, and what the input actually was.

> This function should return unique emails in order. With the input below it returns duplicates.
>
> Code: [code]
> Input: `["A@b.com", "a@b.com"]`
> Expected: `["a@b.com"]`
> Actual: `["A@b.com", "a@b.com"]`
> Error: none, it just returns the wrong thing

That gets a correct answer immediately. "My email function is broken" does not.

### The two kinds of bug

**Loud bugs** raise an error. The traceback names the line and often the cause. These are cheap.

**Quiet bugs** produce wrong output with no error. Nothing tells you. These are what tests exist for, and where AI help is most valuable, because you have to describe the discrepancy and describing it often reveals it.

### Ask for the cause, not just the fix

> Explain what is causing this before giving me a fix.

A fix without a cause teaches nothing and may be wrong in a way you cannot detect. If you cannot explain why the fix works, you have not fixed the bug; you have changed the symptom.

### Rubber-duck debugging, upgraded

Explaining a problem out loud often solves it before anyone answers. That works with a model too, and the model sometimes adds something.

Writing out the four items above is itself a debugging technique. A fair proportion of the time you find the bug while composing the message.

### When it goes in circles

If two or three attempts have not worked, stop. The model is now guessing, and each attempt adds plausible-looking changes that make things worse.

Reset:

- Start a fresh conversation with a clean description
- Reduce the problem to the smallest code that still fails
- Ask it to add logging or print statements rather than a fix, so you can see what is actually happening

That third option is underused and often the fastest route.

### What it cannot do

**It cannot see your environment.** Versions, installed packages, configuration, the actual data. Tell it, or it will guess.

**It cannot run your code** unless you are using a tool that can. Without execution it is reasoning about what should happen.

**It does not know your data.** "It works on my test data and fails on the real data" is usually about the data, which the model has never seen.

## Demonstrate

Here is a quiet bug. Take it to any assistant with the four items.

```python
def average_scores(records):
    """Average score per student."""
    totals = {}
    for record in records:
        name = record["name"]
        totals[name] = totals.get(name, 0) + record["score"]
    return {name: total / len(records) for name, total in totals.items()}
```

Input: `[{"name": "a", "score": 10}, {"name": "a", "score": 20}, {"name": "b", "score": 6}]`
Expected: `{"a": 15.0, "b": 6.0}`
Actual: `{"a": 10.0, "b": 2.0}`

Give it all four items and ask for the **cause before the fix**.

The cause is that it divides by the total number of records rather than the number of records per student. Notice that no error was raised and the output looked like plausible averages -- which is what makes quiet bugs expensive.

## Practice

### Exercise: fix it properly

Fix `average_scores` so it divides by the right count.

```python
def average_scores(records: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Average score per student.

    Each record is a dict with 'name' (str) and 'score' (number).
    Returns an empty dict for an empty input.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for the input above:

```
{'a': 15.0, 'b': 6.0}
```

:::hint Getting started
You need two accumulators, not one: a running total per name and a count per name. Then divide them pairwise at the end. Two dicts, or one dict whose values are `[total, count]` pairs.
:::

:::solution
```python
def average_scores(records: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Average score per student."""
    totals: dict[str, float] = {}
    counts: dict[str, int] = {}

    for record in records:
        name = record["name"]
        totals[name] = totals.get(name, 0.0) + record["score"]
        counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + 1

    return {name: totals[name] / counts[name] for name in totals}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = [
        {"name": "a", "score": 10},
        {"name": "a", "score": 20},
        {"name": "b", "score": 6},
    ]
    print(average_scores(data))
    print(average_scores([]))
```

Output:

```
{'a': 15.0, 'b': 6.0}
{}
```

No guard is needed against division by zero: a name only appears in `totals` if it was counted at least once, so `counts[name]` is never zero. That is worth noticing rather than adding a defensive check that can never fire.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This is meant to find the first duplicate in a list. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def first_duplicate(items):
    seen = []
    for item in items:
        seen.append(item)
        if item in seen:
            return item
    return None
```

:::hint What to look at
Trace it with `[1, 2, 3]`, which has no duplicates at all. Then think about whether the order of the two statements inside the loop is right.
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: the order is wrong.** It appends the item and *then* checks whether it is in `seen` -- which it now always is. Every input returns its first element. The check must come before the append.

**Bug two: `seen` is a list, so `in` is a linear scan.** Correct but slow: on a large input this is quadratic. A set makes it constant-time per lookup.

```python
def first_duplicate(items: list) -> object | None:
    """Return the first item that appears more than once, or None."""
    seen = set()
    for item in items:
        if item in seen:
            return item
        seen.add(item)
    return None
```

Bug one is the important one, and it is a good example of why you run generated code rather than reading it approvingly. The function looks entirely reasonable, has no error, and is wrong for every possible input -- including returning a confident answer for a list with no duplicates in it at all.
:::

## What to remember

- Give it the code, the full error, what you expected and what happened
- Ask for the cause before the fix; a fix you cannot explain is not a fix
- Quiet bugs produce wrong output with no error and are the expensive kind
- After two or three failed attempts, reset rather than continuing
- Ask for logging instead of a fix when you cannot see what is happening

lessons.title: Documentation
lessons.description: Comment the why, not the what -- and never let it invent a rationale.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Documentation is the job everyone agrees matters and nobody wants to do. It is also transformation of code that is right in front of the model, which makes it one of the safer uses.

### What it does well

**Docstrings and comments.** From working code, describing what a function takes, returns and raises.

**README files.** What the project is, how to install it, how to run it, a worked example.

**Explaining the why.** Ask what a piece of code is doing and use the answer as a starting point for a comment.

**Keeping docs in step with code.** Paste the old documentation and the new code and ask what needs updating. This is where documentation usually rots, and it is a genuinely good use.

**Usage examples.** From a function signature, a realistic example of calling it.

### The rule that matters

**Comment the why, not the what.**

Generated comments default to restating the code:

```python
# Loop through the items
for item in items:
    # Add one to the counter
    counter += 1
```

This is worse than nothing. It adds lines, adds something to maintain, and says nothing the code did not already say.

What a reader actually needs is the reason:

```python
# Skip malformed rows rather than raising: one bad row in a nightly
# import should not lose the whole batch.
if not valid(row):
    continue
```

The code says what. Only a person knows why. So ask explicitly:

> Add comments explaining **why** each non-obvious decision was made, not what the code does. Where you cannot tell why, write `# TODO: why?` rather than guessing.

That last clause is important. Without it, the model invents a rationale, and an invented rationale in a comment is worse than no comment -- it will be believed.

### Docstrings

Ask for a specific convention and specific contents:

> Write a docstring in Google style. Include: one-line summary, arguments with types and meaning, return value, and any exception raised. Do not describe the implementation.

"Do not describe the implementation" keeps the docstring useful when the implementation changes.

### READMEs

A good brief:

> Write a README for this project. Sections: what it does in two sentences, installation, a minimal working example, configuration, and how to run the tests.
>
> Use only what you can see in the code. Where something is missing -- a licence, a dependency list -- list it under "missing" rather than inventing it.

The "missing" instruction is the same pattern as module 4's uncertainty rule, and it turns the gaps into a to-do list.

### What it cannot know

**Why the project exists.** The business reason, the history, what was tried before.

**The constraints you were under.** Why the obvious approach was not used.

**The things that bit you.** The subtle failure that led to a strange-looking line.

That context is the most valuable documentation there is, and only you have it. Write those parts yourself.

## Demonstrate

Take a function you have written, or use `totals_by_customer` from lesson 2.

Ask for three things separately and compare:

1. *"Add comments explaining what each line does."*
2. *"Add comments explaining why each non-obvious decision was made. Where you cannot tell why, write `# TODO: why?`"*
3. *"Write a Google-style docstring. Do not describe the implementation."*

Version 1 will be noise. Version 2 will be genuinely useful and will honestly mark the places it could not know. Version 3 will be the thing you keep.

The difference between 1 and 2 is one word in the prompt.

## Practice

Take a real script of yours that has no documentation.

Generate a docstring and why-comments using the prompts above.

Then do the part only you can do: find every `# TODO: why?` and answer it, and add one paragraph at the top saying why this script exists and what it was for.

That paragraph is the most valuable documentation in the file and no tool could have written it.

## What to remember

- Comment the why, not the what; ask explicitly or you get restated code
- Add "write TODO where you cannot tell why" so it does not invent a rationale
- Ask for a named docstring convention and say not to describe the implementation
- Use "list what is missing" rather than letting it invent a licence or dependency
- Only you know why the project exists; write that part yourself

lessons.title: GitHub Copilot in practice
lessons.description: Comment-first prompting, and the habit that forms within a week.
lessons.content:
## Learn

GitHub Copilot is the best-known in-editor assistant. This lesson is about the in-editor experience generally; the specific product matters less than the workflow.

### The three modes

**Inline completion.** Suggestions as you type. Press a key to accept.

**Chat in the editor.** Ask about the open file, with your code as context.

**Multi-file changes.** Describe a change and have it proposed across files.

### Getting good completions

**Write the comment first.** State what you want above where you want it. The comment becomes part of the prompt.

```python
# Return the median of a list of numbers.
# Raise ValueError on an empty list. Do not modify the input.
def median(values: list[float]) -> float:
```

The completion after this is far better than after a bare `def median(`.

**Write the signature with types.** Type hints tell it a great deal about intent.

**Name things well.** `customer_totals` produces better suggestions than `d`.

**Keep related files open.** Editors send open files as context, so having the relevant model or schema open improves suggestions noticeably.

**Write the test first.** A test above your function is a precise specification, and completions become substantially better.

### The habit that matters

**Read every suggestion before accepting.**

This is easy to say and genuinely hard to do. The suggestions are fast, usually reasonable, and pressing Tab is frictionless. Within a week, accepting without reading is a habit.

Two things help:

**Pause on anything longer than a couple of lines.** Short completions are usually safe. Long ones deserve a read.

**Be suspicious when it completes something you had not thought through.** If it wrote the logic before you decided what the logic should be, you are now reviewing a design you did not make.

### What to watch for

**Invented library functions.** Common in smaller libraries. Fails immediately, which makes it one of the cheaper failures.

**Plausible but wrong edge-case handling.** It will confidently handle the empty case in a way you did not want.

**Copying a pattern from elsewhere in your file** that was wrong there too.

**Security-relevant code.** Anything touching authentication, permissions, secrets or user input deserves careful review rather than acceptance. It will produce something that works and is not necessarily safe.

**Secrets.** It can complete a plausible-looking API key. Never let one into a file. Which brings us to the rule from module 4 that applies everywhere in this course:

```python
import os

api_key = os.environ["SERVICE_API_KEY"]   # never a literal
```

### Productivity, honestly

Surveys consistently find real time savings on routine work and much less benefit on hard problems.

That matches the shape of the tool. Boilerplate, tests and familiar patterns speed up a lot. The difficult parts -- deciding what to build, understanding a subtle bug, designing something that will survive change -- are not where it helps.

If your work is mostly the second kind, expect less than the headlines suggest.

## Demonstrate

Whether or not you have an in-editor assistant, do this with any tool.

Write only this, and ask for the implementation:

```python
# Group a list of transaction dicts by month.
# Each transaction has 'date' (YYYY-MM-DD string) and 'amount' (float).
# Return a dict of 'YYYY-MM' to total amount, sorted by month.
# Skip transactions with a malformed date, and return {} for empty input.
def group_by_month(transactions: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:
```

Then, before running it, read it and answer:

1. How does it handle a malformed date? Is that what you wanted?
2. Does it actually sort, or does it rely on insertion order?
3. What happens with an empty list?

Then run it and check your answers.

The gap between what you assumed while reading and what it actually does is the thing this exercise is measuring, and it is usually not zero.

## Practice

Write three comment-first specifications for small functions you actually need.

For each, generate the implementation, then before running it write down what you believe it does about the edge cases.

Run it. Compare your expectations with reality.

Record your accuracy. This calibrates how carefully you need to read, which is a more useful thing to know than any general advice about it.

## What to remember

- Write the comment and the typed signature first; it is a prompt
- Keep related files open, and write the test first for the best results
- Read everything longer than a couple of lines before accepting
- Watch invented library functions, edge-case handling and anything security-relevant
- Never let a secret into a file; read keys from the environment
- Real savings on routine work, much less on hard problems

lessons.title: Project: a small application, built with AI
lessons.description: Build something real, one verifiable function at a time.
lessons.content:
## Learn

This lesson is a project: build something small and working, with AI assistance, using everything in this module. It is deliberately achievable by someone who does not consider themselves a programmer.

### The project

**A command-line tool that reads a CSV of expenses and prints a summary.**

Small enough to finish, real enough to be useful, and it exercises input handling, edge cases, tests and documentation.

Requirements:

- Read a CSV with columns `date`, `category`, `amount`, `description`
- Print the total, the total per category, and the three largest single expenses
- Handle a missing file, an empty file, malformed rows and a bad amount without crashing
- Accept the filename as a command-line argument

### The method: build it in pieces

The most important lesson here. **Do not ask for the whole program.**

Ask for one function at a time, with a clear contract. Read it. Run it. Test it. Then the next.

The order:

1. Read and parse the CSV into a list of records, skipping bad rows
2. Compute the totals
3. Find the largest expenses
4. Format the output
5. Wire up the command-line argument handling
6. Tests for each
7. A README

Each step is small enough to verify. A whole program generated at once is plausible and unverifiable.

### Start with the contract

For each piece, write the signature and docstring first, then ask for the implementation:

```python
import csv
from pathlib import Path


def load_expenses(path: Path) -> tuple[list[dict], list[str]]:
    """Read expenses from a CSV file.

    Returns a tuple of (records, problems). Each record is a dict with
    'date' (str), 'category' (str), 'amount' (float) and 'description'
    (str). Rows that cannot be parsed are skipped and described in
    'problems' rather than raising.

    Raises FileNotFoundError if the path does not exist.
    """
```

Note the return type. Returning the problems rather than printing or discarding them means the caller decides what to do, and it makes the function testable.

### The rules for this project

**Read everything before accepting it.**

**Run every piece before moving on.**

**Write a test for each piece.** At minimum: normal case, empty case, malformed case.

**Ask "what could go wrong with this?" for every function.**

**If you cannot explain a line, ask until you can.** Do not keep code you do not understand.

## Demonstrate

The first piece, done properly, to show the method.

**Step one: ask for it.**

> Python 3.11. Implement this function. Standard library only. Handle: file not found (raise), empty file (return empty lists), a row with a missing column, and a row where amount is not a number. Skip bad rows and describe each in the problems list with the row number. State any assumption in a comment.
>
> [paste the signature and docstring above]

**Step two: read it.** Specifically, check how it detects a bad amount, what it does with a missing column, and whether the row numbers are what a person would expect -- humans count the header as row 1.

**Step three: run it** on a real file, an empty file, and a file with a deliberately broken row.

**Step four: ask what could go wrong.** You will likely be told about encoding, about very large files, and about whitespace around values.

**Step five: write the test.**

Five steps for one function. That is the pace, and it is why building in pieces works.

## Practice

### Exercise: build it

Build the whole tool, piece by piece. Here is the second function to get you going.

```python
def totals_by_category(records: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Total spend per category, highest first.

    Returns a dict ordered from largest total to smallest. An empty
    input returns an empty dict.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output for records totalling 40 on 'food' and 15 on 'travel':

```
{'food': 40.0, 'travel': 15.0}
```

:::hint Getting started
Accumulate into a plain dict first, exactly as in lesson 2. Then sort: `dict(sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True))`. Dicts preserve insertion order in modern Python, so building a new one from the sorted pairs gives you the ordering.
:::

:::solution
```python
def totals_by_category(records: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Total spend per category, highest first."""
    totals: dict[str, float] = {}
    for record in records:
        category = record["category"]
        totals[category] = totals.get(category, 0.0) + record["amount"]

    # Dicts preserve insertion order, so rebuilding from sorted pairs
    # gives a dict that iterates highest-first.
    return dict(sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rows = [
        {"category": "food", "amount": 25.0},
        {"category": "travel", "amount": 15.0},
        {"category": "food", "amount": 15.0},
    ]
    print(totals_by_category(rows))
```

Output:

```
{'food': 40.0, 'travel': 15.0}
```

This assumes `load_expenses` already guaranteed every record has both keys with the right types -- which is why that function returns problems separately rather than passing bad rows through. Each function trusting the contract of the one before it is what keeps them small.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This is meant to find the three largest expenses. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def largest_expenses(records, n=3):
    records.sort(key=lambda r: r["amount"], reverse=True)
    return records[0:n]
```

:::hint What to look at
Two things. First, what does `list.sort` do to the list you were given? Second, what happens if there are fewer than `n` records -- and is that actually a problem?
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: it mutates the caller's list.** `list.sort` sorts in place, so the caller's records are reordered as a side effect. A function that quietly rearranges its argument causes bugs somewhere else entirely, which are very hard to trace back. Use `sorted()`, which returns a new list.

**Bug two is not the slice.** `records[0:3]` on a two-item list returns two items, which is correct and needs no guard. The second real bug is the **missing type hints and docstring**, which the project's own rules required -- and more substantively, that `n` is not validated: `largest_expenses(records, -1)` silently returns an empty list rather than complaining.

```python
def largest_expenses(records: list[dict], n: int = 3) -> list[dict]:
    """The n largest expenses, highest first. Does not modify the input."""
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must not be negative")
    return sorted(records, key=lambda record: record["amount"], reverse=True)[:n]
```

Bug one is the one worth remembering. Generated code frequently uses in-place operations where a copy was wanted, because in isolation the code looks correct -- the damage appears in a different function, later, and looks like a bug there.
:::

## What to remember

- Build in pieces with clear contracts; never ask for the whole program
- Write the signature and docstring first, then ask for the implementation
- Run every piece before moving to the next
- Return problems rather than printing or discarding them
- Watch for functions that quietly modify their arguments
- If you cannot explain a line, do not keep it

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
Ten questions on the whole of module 9.

:::quiz
Q. Which use of a coding assistant is most valuable to someone who does not write code?
- Generating new programs from scratch
+ Explaining code they did not write
- Writing tests
- Refactoring for performance
= Explanation is transformation of code that is right in front of the model, which is the safe category. It makes inherited scripts and unfamiliar code far less intimidating, and it needs no ability to write code yourself.

Q. What is the single best question to ask about a piece of code?
- "Can you make this shorter?"
+ "What could go wrong with this?"
- "Is this good code?"
- "How fast is this?"
= It surfaces edge cases, failure modes and assumptions you would not have thought to ask about. The value is in the cases it raises, even when you disagree with its judgement about them.

Q. What must a debugging request contain to get a useful answer?
- The code and a description of the problem
+ The code, the full error, what you expected, and what actually happened
- The code and the input data
- The error message and the line number
= Missing any of the four makes the answer a guess. The model cannot know your intent, so "what you expected" is not optional. Writing these four out often reveals the bug before you send it.

Q. What makes a quiet bug more expensive than a loud one?
- It takes longer to fix
+ It produces wrong output with no error, so nothing tells you it is there
- It only appears in production
- It cannot be found by AI assistants
= A loud bug names its own line in the traceback. A quiet one returns plausible-looking wrong answers indefinitely. This is why you run generated code rather than reading it approvingly.

Q. Generated comments default to restating the code. What should you ask for instead?
- Shorter comments
+ Comments explaining why each non-obvious decision was made, with TODO where it cannot tell
- Comments only on complex lines
- Docstrings instead of comments
= The code already says what. Only a person knows why. Without the TODO clause the model invents a rationale, and an invented rationale in a comment is worse than no comment because it will be believed.

Q. Why write the comment and typed signature before asking for an implementation?
- It makes the code easier to read afterwards
+ They are part of the prompt, and they specify intent the model cannot otherwise know
- It is required by most editors
- It prevents the model from changing the function name
= A bare `def median(` gives the model almost nothing. A comment stating the behaviour and edge cases, plus type hints, produces markedly better completions. Writing the test first works for the same reason.

Q. What should you do after two or three failed debugging attempts?
- Give the model more of the codebase
+ Reset: fresh conversation, smallest failing example, or ask for logging rather than a fix
- Switch to a more capable model
- Ask it to try harder
= After a few failures the model is guessing, and each attempt layers plausible changes that make things worse. Asking for logging instead of a fix, so you can see what is actually happening, is the most underused option.

Q. Why build a project one function at a time rather than asking for the whole program?
- It uses fewer tokens
+ Each piece is small enough to read, run and test; a whole program is plausible and unverifiable
- The model cannot produce a whole program
- It produces faster code
= This is the central discipline of the module. A generated program looks right and cannot be meaningfully checked. Five small steps per function feels slow and is far faster overall.

Q. A generated function uses `list.sort` on its argument. What is the problem?
- `sort` is slower than `sorted`
+ It modifies the caller's list as a side effect, causing bugs elsewhere that are hard to trace
- `sort` cannot take a key function
- It fails on empty lists
= Generated code frequently uses in-place operations where a copy was wanted, because in isolation it looks correct. The damage shows up in a different function later and looks like a bug there.

Q. What does the evidence suggest about productivity gains from coding assistants?
- Large gains across all kinds of work
+ Real gains on routine work, much less on hard problems
- Gains only for experienced programmers
- No measurable difference
= This matches the shape of the tool. Boilerplate, tests and familiar patterns speed up considerably. Deciding what to build, understanding a subtle bug and designing for change are not where it helps.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for module 10. If you missed questions, the most useful correction is to go and do the debugging exercises rather than reread -- this module's lessons only stick once you have had generated code fail on you.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: fix four broken programs
lessons.description: Four bugs, four ways of announcing themselves, one diagnostic method.
lessons.content:
Forty-five minutes. Four programs, each broken, each in a different way. You will fix all four using the method from lesson 4, and record what happened.

The goal is not to fix them -- the fixes are small. It is to practise the diagnostic method and to notice how differently each kind of bug announces itself.

## Before you start

You need Python and any AI assistant. Create a file for each program and run it before you change anything, so you see the real behaviour.

Keep a record with, for each program: how the bug announced itself, what you gave the assistant, what it said the cause was, whether it was right, and what the fix was.

## Program 1: a loud bug

```python
def read_config(path):
    settings = {}
    for line in open(path):
        key, value = line.strip().split("=")
        settings[key] = value
    return settings


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(read_config("config.txt"))
```

`config.txt`:

```
name=report
rows=50
# this is a comment
output=out.csv
```

Run it. Note the exact error. Then debug it properly with all four items from lesson 4.

## Program 2: a quiet bug

```python
def apply_discount(prices, percent):
    """Reduce each price by percent. Returns the new list."""
    for i in range(len(prices)):
        prices[i] = prices[i] - (prices[i] * percent / 100)
    return prices


if __name__ == "__main__":
    original = [100.0, 250.0, 80.0]
    discounted = apply_discount(original, 10)
    print("discounted:", discounted)
    print("original:  ", original)
```

No error. Run it and look carefully at both printed lines.

:::hint What am I looking for
Compare the two printed lines. The function was documented as returning a new list. Did it?
:::

## Program 3: a bug that only appears sometimes

```python
import random


def pick_winners(entries, count=3):
    """Pick `count` distinct winners from entries."""
    winners = []
    while len(winners) < count:
        choice = random.choice(entries)
        if choice not in winners:
            winners.append(choice)
    return winners


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(pick_winners(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]))
    print(pick_winners(["a", "b"]))
```

The first call works. Run the second one.

This is the most instructive of the four: a bug that depends on the input, does not raise, and does not even finish.

## Program 4: a bug in the logic, not the code

```python
def is_valid_password(password: str) -> bool:
    """A password is valid if it is at least 8 characters,
    contains a digit, and contains an uppercase letter."""
    if len(password) < 8:
        return False
    if any(c.isdigit() for c in password):
        return True
    if any(c.isupper() for c in password):
        return True
    return False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for candidate in ["short1A", "alllowercase1", "ALLUPPERCASE1", "Valid1234", "nodigitsHere"]:
        print(f"{candidate!r}: {is_valid_password(candidate)}")
```

Run it. Work out what it should print, then compare.

The code does exactly what it says. What it says is not what the docstring promised.

## For each program

1. **Run it first.** Record the actual behaviour.
2. **Write the four items**: code, full error or observed behaviour, what you expected, what happened.
3. **Ask for the cause before the fix.**
4. **Judge the answer.** Was the stated cause right? Did it also mention anything you had missed?
5. **Apply the fix and rerun.**
6. **Write a test** that would have caught it.

Step 6 matters. A bug you have fixed without a test is a bug that can come back.

## Write it up

For each of the four:

- How the bug announced itself: loudly, quietly, intermittently, or as a logic error
- What the assistant said the cause was, and whether it was right
- Your fix
- The test you wrote

Then two paragraphs:

1. Which of the four was hardest to diagnose, and why
2. Which kind of bug do you think you are most likely to ship, and what habit would catch it

## What good looks like

A strong write-up **judges the assistant's answer** rather than just applying it. It was right about some and possibly wrong or incomplete about others; saying which is the point of the exercise.

It also has four real tests. A test that would not actually have failed before the fix is not a test of that bug — check by running it against the original code.

lessons.title: Assignment: build and document a small tool
lessons.description: A working tool plus an honest account of where the assistant was wrong.
lessons.content:
## The task

Build a small, working, documented tool with AI assistance -- and document how you used the assistance, including where it got things wrong.

The tool is the deliverable. The account of building it is what is being marked most heavily.

## What to build

Something small, real and useful to you. It must:

- Do one clear thing
- Take input from a file or the command line
- Handle at least four failure cases without crashing
- Have tests
- Have a README

Some that work well: a CSV summariser; a tool that renames files by a rule; a study-question generator from a text file; a script that checks a folder of documents against a checklist; a simple habit or expense tracker; a tool that extracts structured data from messy text.

If you prefer, build the expenses tool from lesson 7 properly.

**It must run.** A submission that raises on import cannot pass.

## What to submit

The code, plus a document of **900 to 1300 words**.

### The code

- The tool itself, in one or more Python files
- Tests, covering at minimum the normal case and every failure case you claim to handle
- A README: what it does, how to run it, a worked example, and what is missing

**No hard-coded secrets.** If your tool uses any API, read the key from the environment with `os.environ`. A key in a submitted file loses marks and is a real security problem.

### The document

**1. What it does and why you built it.** One paragraph.

**2. How you broke it into pieces.** The functions, their contracts, and the order you built them. Show that you did not ask for the whole program.

**3. Three prompts you used, in full.** With a note on what each produced and what you had to change.

**4. Where the assistant got it wrong.** The heaviest-marked section.

**At least three** specific errors, each with:

- What it produced
- Why it was wrong
- How you noticed
- What you did about it

Errors that count: a quiet bug, an invented function, wrong edge-case handling, a function that mutated its argument, a plausible explanation that turned out to be inaccurate, a test that passed for the wrong reason.

"It got everything right" is not a credible claim across a whole project and scores nothing here.

**5. One thing you did not understand, and how you resolved it.** Everyone hits a line they cannot follow. Show the line, show what you asked, show that you now understand it.

**6. Your tests.** What each covers and which bug it would catch. For at least one, confirm you ran it against the broken version and watched it fail.

**7. Honest assessment.** How long did it take? What would it have taken without assistance? Where did the assistant genuinely help, and where did it cost you time?

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**The tool, 20 marks.** Full marks for a tool that runs, does what the README says, and handles its four failure cases without crashing. Marks lost for each claimed failure case that actually crashes.

**Decomposition, 10 marks.** Full marks for a clear breakdown into functions with stated contracts, built in order. Marks lost where the account suggests the whole thing was generated at once.

**Prompts, 10 marks.** Full marks for three full prompts showing the ingredients from lesson 2 -- language, input, output, edge cases, constraints. Marks lost for prompts that are one vague sentence.

**Where it got it wrong, 25 marks.** Full marks for three or more specific errors with what, why, how you noticed and what you did. The heaviest section. A submission claiming no errors scores zero here regardless of how good the tool is.

**The line you did not understand, 10 marks.** Full marks for a real example where you can now explain it.

**Tests, 15 marks.** Full marks for tests covering the normal case and every claimed failure case, with at least one confirmed to fail against the broken version. Marks lost for tests that would pass against the original buggy code.

**Honest assessment, 10 marks.** Full marks for a genuine account including where assistance cost time. Marks lost for an assessment that reports only benefits.

## What will cost you marks

**A tool that does not run.** Check on a clean copy before submitting.

**Claiming no errors.** Across a whole project this is not believable and costs a quarter of the marks.

**Tests that do not test.** A test that passes against the buggy original has not tested anything. Run them against the broken version and say so.

**Code you cannot explain.** If asked about any line, you should be able to say what it does. Keeping code you do not understand is the exact failure this module is designed to prevent.

**A hard-coded key.** Checked for, and costs marks in two sections.

:::hint I do not code and this feels out of reach
It is more achievable than it looks, and the module is built for this. Start with the smallest possible version: one function that reads a file and prints how many lines it has. Get that running. Then add one thing at a time, running it after each. The assignment does not require a large tool -- it requires a small one you genuinely understand, with an honest account of building it. A three-function tool you can fully explain scores far higher than a large one you cannot.
:::
